- Chemometrics is the application of mathematics and statistics to chemical *measurements*

- In practice, this mostly means creating algorithms to: - process and interpret single measurements
- compare and contrast multiple measurements
- compile multiple measurements as databases (libraries) - search libraries - classify measurements ::: {.notes} ::: ## Searching measurement libraries - Let $\mathbf{X}=\{X_1, X_2,...,X_n\}$ be a library of measurements

- Let $U$ be the measurement of an unknown

- Let $d_i = f(U,X_i)$ be the numerical **distance** between the unknown measurement and library measurement $i$

- In library searching, we compute $\mathbf{d} = (d_1, d_2, ..., d_n)$ ## Searching measurement libraries - We then generate a **Hit List** of the top $k$ most similar measurements from the library

$\mathbf{H}=\text{top}_k(\text{sort}(\mathbf{X},\text{by } \mathbf{d}))$

- We inspect $\mathbf{H}$ and try to determine which (if any) of the measurements in $\mathbf{H}$: 1. are a potential identity for $U$, or 1. have information that can help us interpret $U$ ## Searching measurement libraries - Start by clearing work space, loading custom functions, and loading a pre-compiled library (note to arun, explain the library structure to students)

:::{.fragment} ```{r} #| eval: false ## Step 0. Clear up the work space, load custom functions, load the reference mass spectral library rm(list=ls()) # clears up the work space source("CustomFunctions/LibrarySearchFunctions.R") # loads all the functions in the file Library = readRDS("asm_ReferenceMSLibrary_SWDRUG314.RDS") # loads the reference library ``` ::: ## Searching measurement libraries - Load up an unknown, define the metric used to compare the unknown to the library spectra, and define the number of results that will be returned as a hit list

:::{.fragment} ```{r} #| eval: false Unknown = read.table("Unknowns/U1.txt") # reads in the unknown mass spectrum Metric = "Euclidean" # this can take one of two values "Euclidean" or "CosineSim" nHits = 10 # this is the number of most similar library entries we want returned Results = LibrarySearch(Unknown,Library,Metric,nHits) # This returns the library search HitList and RunTime. View(Results$HitList) cat(Results$RunTime) ``` ::: ## Library Search (Under-the-hood)
```{r} #| eval: false LibrarySearch <- function(Unknown,Library,Metric,nHits){ Unknown[,2] = Unknown[,2]/max(Unknown[,2]) # normalizes the relative intensity of the unknown mass spectrum nSearch = dim(Library$IndexData)[1] # determines the number of library entries (i.e., number of comparisons) Name = character(nSearch) Score = numeric(nSearch) mzU = Unknown[,1] relU = Unknown[,2] stime <- system.time({ #cat("Library Search in progress... ") for(i in 1:nSearch){ index = Library$IndexData$ID[i] indices = which(Library$SpectralData$SpecID==index) mzL = Library$SpectralData$mz[indices] relL = Library$SpectralData$int[indices] relL = relL/max(relL) # make sure intensities are normalized max_mz = max_mz = max(max(mzU),max(mzL)) vecU = spec2vec(mzU,relU,max_mz) vecL = spec2vec(mzL,relL,max_mz) Name[i] = Library$IndexData$Name[i] if(Metric=="Euclidean"){ Score[i] = euclideanDistance(vecU,vecL) } else if (Metric=="CosineSim"){ Score[i] = cosineSim(vecU,vecL) } else { cat("ERROR: Inappropriate Metric selection.\n\n") return(NULL) } } })[3] #cat(paste("Library search complete! Elapsed time: ",round(stime,3)," seconds.")) if(Metric=="Euclidean"){ Sort = order(Score,decreasing=FALSE) } else if (Metric=="CosineSim") { Sort = order(Score,decreasing=TRUE) } Result = data.frame(Name = Name[Sort],Score = Score[Sort]) return(list(HitList = Result[1:nHits,], RunTime = paste0("Elapsed time: ",round(stime,3)," seconds."))) } ``` ## More on library searches - Library searches are $O(n)$ time-complex algorithms, this means they scale linearly with the size of the problem - E.g., if it takes 10 seconds to search a library with 10 entries, it will take 3600 seconds to search library with 3600 entries

- Most of the entries in your library won't be relevant, especially if you are using a big commercial library

- Using a clever "pre-search" (i.e., a filter to make your library smaller) will help speed up your library search algorithm :::{.notes} Time permits, show the students NIST MS Search via remote access ::: ## Distance Matrices and Multidimensional scaling - In a library search, we compare one unknown to a library of $n$ entries; this tells us how similar the unknown is to each element of the library - It does not tell us how similar the library entries are too each other

- Given a set of measurement (e.g., a library or otherwise), it can be informative to compute an $n\times n$ **distance matrix** $\mathbf{D}$ from $\mathbf{X}$ such that

$D_{i,j} = d(X_i,X_j)$

- This matrix is the input to several useful algorithms ## A first distance matrix
```{r} #| eval: false U = seq(1,30) D = array(0,dim=c(length(U),length(U))) for(i in 1:length(U)){ indices_i = which(Library$SpectralData$SpecID==U[i]) spec_mz_i = Library$SpectralData$mz[indices_i] spec_int = Library$SpectralData$int[indices_i] spec_int_i = spec_int/max(spec_int) for(j in 1:length(U)){ indices_j = which(Library$SpectralData$SpecID==U[j]) spec_mz_j = Library$SpectralData$mz[indices_j] spec_int = Library$SpectralData$int[indices_j] spec_int_j = spec_int/max(spec_int) maxmz = max(spec_mz_i,spec_mz_j) A = spec2vec(spec_mz_i,spec_int_i,maxmz) B = spec2vec(spec_mz_j,spec_int_j,maxmz) D[i,j] = 1-cosineSim(A,B) } } ``` ## A dendrogram (hierarchical clustering) - a fun algorithm for grouping together measurements based on minimal distance is called agglomerative hierarchical clustering (AHC) - every measurement starts as its own cluster - the two closest clusters are combined, then the next two, then the next two... until there is one big agglomerate cluster - analyst needs to define "closest" in the clustering space

::: {.fragment} ```{r} #| eval: FALSE D = as.dist(D) ClusterResults = hclust(D,method="complete") plot(ClusterResults) ``` ::: ## Multidimensional Scaling - multidimensional scaling is an algorithm that identifies a $k$-dimensional configuration that maintains the gives the same (or near same) distance matrix as the original distance matrix; $k$ is some selected dimensionality of the output configuration

::: {.fragment} ```{r} #| eval: FALSE mds = cmdscale(D,k=2) rownames(mds) = U plot(mds,pch=19,cex=0) text(mds[,1],mds[,2],U) ``` ::: ## Principal Component Analysis - principal component analysis (PCA) is an incredibly popular method for projecting higher dimensional data into a lower dimensional space

::: {.fragment} ```{r} #| eval: FALSE U = seq(1,30) data = array(0,dim=c(length(U),1000)) for(i in 1:length(U)){ indices = which(Library$SpectralData$SpecID==i) mz = Library$SpectralData$mz[indices] int = Library$SpectralData$int[indices] data[i,] = spec2vec(mz,int,1000) } zeros = which(colSums(data)==0) data = data[,-zeros] pca_results = prcomp(data) scores = pca_results$x[,1:2,drop=FALSE] plot(scores,cex=0) text(scores[,1],scores[,2],U) ``` ::: ## Coming up - Seminars are NOT running tomorrow (November 12th)
- I'll be at Market Hall for the Poole Lecture: [A Hard Days’ Math: The Connections Between Mathematics and Music](https://momentous.trentu.ca/poolelectures){target="_blank"}

- **Next week:** A little bit of classification; Working with chemical structures - For *some* of the examples I'll present, I may use a package that requires [JDK](https://www.oracle.com/ca-en/java/technologies/downloads/){target="_blank"} installed on my computer
